en: I have had a fever since yesterday morning.
tamil: எனக்கு நேத்து காலையிலிருந்து காய்ச்சல் இருக்கு.
context: Telling a doctor how long you have been sick.
explain: 'Have had ... since' tells how long a problem has continued up to now.
usage: Use it in a clinic when the doctor asks about your illness.
leelaQ: Have you ever had a high fever? What did you do?
answer: Yes, I had a high fever last year, so I took rest and went to a doctor.

en: My head hurts a lot today.
tamil: இன்னைக்கு எனக்கு தலை ரொம்ப வலிக்குது.
context: Telling a friend or boss you have a headache.
explain: 'Hurts' is a simple present verb for pain. 'A lot' shows the pain is strong.
usage: Say it to a colleague or teacher when you feel unwell.
leelaQ: What do you do when you have a headache?
answer: I drink some water, take a tablet and sleep for a while.

en: How long have you had this cough?
tamil: இந்த இருமல் உங்களுக்கு எவ்வளவு நாளா இருக்கு?
context: A doctor asking about your cough.
explain: 'How long have you had ...?' asks about the duration of a problem.
usage: A doctor or nurse asks this at the start of a check-up.
leelaQ: How long have you had your cough, or when did you last have one?
answer: I have had it for three days, and it is getting better now.

en: Please give me an appointment for tomorrow evening.
tamil: நாளைக்கு சாயங்காலம் எனக்கு ஒரு அப்பாயின்ட்மென்ட் குடுங்க.
context: Asking a clinic receptionist for a time slot.
explain: 'Please give me ...' is a polite way to ask for something at a counter.
usage: Say it at a clinic reception desk or on a phone call.
leelaQ: What will you say to the receptionist to book a time?
answer: I will say, please give me an appointment for tomorrow evening.

en: I could not sleep at all last night.
tamil: நேத்து ராத்திரி என்னால கொஞ்சம் கூட தூங்க முடியல.
context: Telling a doctor about sleep trouble.
explain: 'Could not' talks about something you were unable to do in the past. 'At all' makes it stronger.
usage: Use it with a doctor, a friend or your family when you feel tired.
leelaQ: Did you sleep well last night? Why or why not?
answer: No, I could not sleep well because it was very hot.

en: The doctor will see you in ten minutes.
tamil: டாக்டர் பத்து நிமிஷத்துல உங்களைப் பார்ப்பாரு.
context: A receptionist telling a patient to wait.
explain: 'Will see you' is a polite, formal way to say the doctor is coming. 'In ten minutes' gives the time.
usage: Receptionists and nurses say this in waiting rooms.
leelaQ: How do you feel when you wait a long time at a hospital?
answer: I feel bored and a little worried, so I check my phone.

en: Could you write down the names of the tablets for me?
tamil: மாத்திரைகளோட பேரை எனக்கு எழுதிக் குடுக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a doctor or pharmacist to write the medicine names.
explain: 'Could you ...?' is a very polite request. 'Write down' means to note on paper.
usage: Use it with a doctor or pharmacist when you cannot remember details.
leelaQ: Do you remember the names of medicines you take? Which ones?
answer: I remember only paracetamol, because I take it for fever.

en: Do you have any allergies to medicines?
tamil: உங்களுக்கு ஏதாவது மருந்து அலர்ஜி இருக்கா?
context: A doctor or pharmacist checking for allergies.
explain: 'Do you have any ...?' is a common way to ask about conditions. 'Allergies' is the plural noun.
usage: Doctors ask this before giving a new tablet or injection.
leelaQ: Are you allergic to any food or medicine?
answer: No, I am not allergic to anything, but my brother is allergic to dust.

en: I am taking these tablets twice a day after food.
tamil: நான் இந்த மாத்திரைகளை தினமும் ரெண்டு தடவை சாப்பிட்டு அப்புறம் போடுறேன்.
context: Explaining your medicine routine to a doctor.
explain: 'Am taking' shows a medicine course that is going on now. 'Twice a day' tells how often.
usage: Say it when a doctor asks about the medicines you are using.
leelaQ: How often do you take medicine when you are sick?
answer: I take it two times a day, once in the morning and once at night.

en: I went to the clinic near my house this morning.
tamil: நான் இன்னைக்கு காலையில வீட்டுக்கு பக்கத்துல இருக்கிற கிளினிக்குக்கு போனேன்.
context: Telling a friend where you went today.
explain: 'Went' is the past form of 'go'. 'This morning' shows the time of the action.
usage: Use it when you tell family or colleagues why you came late.
leelaQ: Where do you go when you are not well?
answer: I go to a small clinic near my house, because it is very close.

en: Is it a serious problem, doctor?
tamil: இது ஏதாவது பெரிய பிரச்சனையா டாக்டர்?
context: Asking the doctor about your condition.
explain: Starting with 'Is it ...?' makes a simple yes-or-no question. Adding 'doctor' is respectful.
usage: Ask this when you feel worried after a check-up.
leelaQ: What do you ask the doctor when you feel worried?
answer: I ask if it is serious and how many days it will take to recover.

en: You should drink plenty of warm water and take rest.
tamil: நீங்க நிறைய சூடான தண்ணி குடிச்சு ஓய்வு எடுக்கணும்.
context: A doctor or elder giving simple advice.
explain: 'Should' gives advice. 'Plenty of' means a lot of something.
usage: Use it to advise a friend or family member who has a cold.
leelaQ: What advice will you give a friend who has a cold?
answer: I will tell him to drink warm water, take rest and avoid cold drinks.

en: My mother has high blood pressure, so she checks it every week.
tamil: எங்கம்மாவுக்கு ஹை பிளட் பிரஷர் இருக்கு, அதனால வாரா வாரம் செக் பண்றாங்க.
context: Talking about a family member's health.
explain: 'So' joins a cause and its result. 'Every week' shows a habit in simple present.
usage: Use it when someone asks about your family's health.
leelaQ: Does anyone in your family check their health regularly?
answer: Yes, my father checks his sugar level every month.

en: Take this tablet after lunch and dinner.
tamil: இந்த மாத்திரையை மதியமும் ராத்திரியும் சாப்பிட்ட பிறகு போடுங்க.
context: A pharmacist explaining how to use a medicine.
explain: An imperative gives clear instructions. 'After' tells the time to take the tablet.
usage: Pharmacists and doctors say this when they hand over medicines.
leelaQ: How will you tell your grandmother when to take her tablet?
answer: I will say, please take this tablet after lunch and after dinner.

en: Don't skip your breakfast, it is not good for your health.
tamil: காலை சாப்பாட்டை தவிர்க்காதே, அது உடம்புக்கு நல்லது இல்ல.
context: Advising a friend who often skips breakfast.
explain: 'Don't' plus a verb tells someone not to do something. 'Skip' means to miss.
usage: Use it kindly with friends, younger family members or colleagues.
leelaQ: Do you have breakfast every day? What do you usually eat?
answer: Yes, I eat idli or dosa with chutney every morning.

en: Where can I get this blood test done?
tamil: இந்த ரத்த பரிசோதனையை நான் எங்க பண்ணிக்கலாம்?
context: Asking a nurse or a pharmacist about a lab.
explain: 'Get ... done' means to have someone do it for you. 'Can' asks about possibility.
usage: Use it at a hospital reception or a medical shop.
leelaQ: Have you ever done a blood test? Where did you do it?
answer: Yes, I did one at a lab near my office last year.

en: I will come for a check-up next week.
tamil: நான் அடுத்த வாரம் செக்-அப்புக்கு வருவேன்.
context: Promising a doctor you will return.
explain: 'Will come' shows a plan or promise. 'Check-up' is a regular health examination.
usage: Say it at the end of a doctor visit before you leave.
leelaQ: When was your last health check-up?
answer: It was about six months ago, at a hospital near my home.

en: The pharmacy is open until ten at night.
tamil: மெடிக்கல் ஷாப் ராத்திரி பத்து மணி வரைக்கும் திறந்திருக்கும்.
context: Telling someone where they can buy medicine late.
explain: 'Until' tells the last time something is open. 'Is open' describes the shop's state.
usage: Use it when a neighbour or friend needs medicine in the evening.
leelaQ: Is there a medical shop near your house? How far is it?
answer: Yes, there is one just two minutes from my house.

en: Did you take your medicine after food?
tamil: நீ சாப்பிட்ட பிறகு மருந்து சாப்பிட்டியா?
context: Checking if a family member took their tablet.
explain: 'Did you take ...?' asks about a finished action. The main verb stays in base form.
usage: Use it with parents, children or friends who are on medication.
leelaQ: Do you ever forget to take your medicine? What do you do then?
answer: Sometimes I forget, so I set an alarm on my phone.

en: My son has got a sore throat and a runny nose.
tamil: என் பையனுக்கு தொண்டை வலியும் மூக்கு ஒழுகலும் இருக்கு.
context: Describing your child's cold to a doctor.
explain: 'Has got' is a common spoken way to say 'has'. It lists two symptoms with 'and'.
usage: Use it with a doctor or a teacher when a child is ill.
leelaQ: What are the signs of a common cold?
answer: A cold gives you a runny nose, a sore throat and a little cough.

en: I am feeling much better after taking rest.
tamil: ஓய்வு எடுத்ததுக்கு அப்புறம் நான் ரொம்ப நல்லா உணர்றேன்.
context: Telling a colleague you have recovered.
explain: 'Much better' compares with how you felt before. 'After taking' joins a time and an action.
usage: Say it when someone asks how you are after an illness.
leelaQ: How do you feel today compared to yesterday?
answer: I feel much better today because I slept well.

en: Can you check my blood pressure once?
tamil: என்னோட ரத்த அழுத்தத்தை ஒரு தடவை செக் பண்ணிப் பாக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a nurse or pharmacist for a quick check.
explain: 'Can you ...?' is a friendly request. 'Once' means 'one time' in Indian English.
usage: Ask this at a pharmacy, a clinic or a health camp.
leelaQ: What small health check can you do at home?
answer: I can check my weight and my temperature at home.

en: The nurse took my weight and height first.
tamil: நர்ஸ் முதல்ல என் எடையையும் உயரத்தையும் எடுத்தாங்க.
context: Describing what happened at a clinic.
explain: 'Took' is the past of 'take'. 'First' shows the order of what happened.
usage: Use it when you tell someone about your hospital visit.
leelaQ: What happens first when you go to a hospital?
answer: First, I write my name at the counter and then I wait for my turn.

en: I need to fast for eight hours before the blood test.
tamil: ரத்த பரிசோதனைக்கு முன்னாடி நான் எட்டு மணி நேரம் சாப்பிடாம இருக்கணும்.
context: Telling a friend about lab test rules.
explain: 'Need to' shows something that is necessary. 'Fast' means to stay without food.
usage: Use it to explain why you cannot eat before a lab test.
leelaQ: Have you ever fasted for a test or for a festival?
answer: Yes, I fasted for a blood test, and I only had water.

en: I am not allergic to any medicine.
tamil: எனக்கு எந்த மருந்தும் அலர்ஜி இல்ல.
context: Telling a doctor you have no medicine allergy.
explain: 'Allergic to' is the correct phrase with 'to'. 'Not ... any' means none.
usage: Say it when a doctor or a pharmacist asks about allergies.
leelaQ: What foods or things do you avoid because of allergy?
answer: I avoid dust because it makes me sneeze.

en: I walk for thirty minutes every morning before work.
tamil: நான் தினமும் காலையில வேலைக்கு முன்னாடி முப்பது நிமிஷம் நடப்பேன்.
context: Talking about your fitness habit.
explain: Simple present shows a daily habit. 'For thirty minutes' gives the length of time.
usage: Use it when friends or colleagues ask about your routine.
leelaQ: Do you exercise in the morning? What do you do?
answer: Yes, I walk near my house for thirty minutes every day.

en: What time do you normally switch off the lights at night?
tamil: நீங்க பொதுவா ராத்திரி எத்தனை மணிக்கு லைட் அணைப்பீங்க?
context: Asking a friend about their sleep habit.
explain: 'Normally' sits before the main verb. 'Switch off' means to turn something off.
usage: Use it in a casual talk with a friend or a family member.
leelaQ: When do you switch off your phone at night?
answer: I switch off my phone around ten thirty every night.

en: I have started going to the gym near my office.
tamil: நான் என் ஆபீஸ் பக்கத்துல இருக்கிற ஜிம்முக்கு போக ஆரம்பிச்சிருக்கேன்.
context: Telling a colleague about a new habit.
explain: 'Have started' tells something new that is still continuing. 'Going' follows 'started'.
usage: Say it when someone notices you look fit or asks about your day.
leelaQ: Do you want to join a gym? Why or why not?
answer: Yes, I want to, because I sit all day at my desk.

en: I never drink coffee after six in the evening.
tamil: நான் சாயங்காலம் ஆறு மணிக்கு மேல காபி குடிக்கவே மாட்டேன்.
context: Explaining your habit to a friend.
explain: 'Never' is placed before the main verb. It means not at any time.
usage: Use it when someone offers you coffee late and you want to refuse.
leelaQ: Which drink do you avoid at night?
answer: I avoid tea and coffee at night because I cannot sleep.

en: Drinking enough water keeps you fresh all day.
tamil: தேவையான தண்ணி குடிச்சா நாள் முழுக்க ஃப்ரெஷ்ஷா இருக்கலாம்.
context: Giving a friend a simple health tip.
explain: 'Drinking' works like a noun at the start of the sentence. 'Keeps you fresh' is the result.
usage: Use it as friendly advice with colleagues or family.
leelaQ: How many glasses of water do you drink in a day?
answer: I drink around eight glasses, but sometimes I forget.

en: Please remind me to take my tablet at night.
tamil: ராத்திரி என் மாத்திரையை சாப்பிட ஞாபகப்படுத்துங்க, ப்ளீஸ்.
context: Asking a family member for a reminder.
explain: 'Remind me to ...' asks someone to help you remember. 'Please' keeps it polite.
usage: Say it to your spouse, parents or a roommate.
leelaQ: Who reminds you when you forget something important?
answer: My wife reminds me, and sometimes my phone alarm also helps.

en: I lost three kilos in two months by eating less rice.
tamil: நான் சாதம் குறைவா சாப்பிட்டு ரெண்டு மாசத்துல மூணு கிலோ குறைஞ்சேன்.
context: Sharing your weight loss story.
explain: 'By eating' tells the method used. 'Lost' is the past form of 'lose'.
usage: Use it when friends ask how you became slim.
leelaQ: What small change in food can help a person stay healthy?
answer: Eating less oily food and more vegetables can help a lot.

en: How many hours of sleep do you get on weekdays?
tamil: வாரநாட்கள்ல நீங்க எத்தனை மணி நேரம் தூங்குவீங்க?
context: Asking a colleague about sleep.
explain: 'How many hours' asks for a number. 'Get' here means to receive or have.
usage: Use it in a normal chat about work and health.
leelaQ: How many hours do you sleep on Sundays?
answer: I sleep for about nine hours on Sundays, because I wake up late.

en: I will start jogging from next Monday.
tamil: நான் அடுத்த திங்கள்கிழமையிலிருந்து ஜாகிங் போகப் போறேன்.
context: Telling a friend your fitness plan.
explain: 'Will start' shows a decision. 'From next Monday' gives the starting day.
usage: Say it when you decide to begin a new healthy habit.
leelaQ: What new healthy habit do you want to start soon?
answer: I want to start doing yoga every morning from next month.

en: My doctor told me to cut down on sugar and oil.
tamil: என் டாக்டர் சர்க்கரையையும் எண்ணெயையும் குறைக்கச் சொன்னாரு.
context: Explaining a diet change to a friend.
explain: 'Told me to ...' reports a doctor's advice. 'Cut down on' means to reduce.
usage: Use it when you refuse sweets or fried food politely.
leelaQ: What food do you want to eat less of?
answer: I want to eat fewer sweets, because I like them too much.

en: We are doing yoga in the park every Sunday.
tamil: நாங்க ஒவ்வொரு ஞாயிற்றுக்கிழமையும் பார்க்குல யோகா பண்றோம்.
context: Inviting a friend to a group activity.
explain: Present continuous can talk about a regular plan that is going on these days. 'We' means a group.
usage: Use it to tell neighbours or friends about a group activity.
leelaQ: Where can people do exercise near your home?
answer: People walk or do yoga in the park near my house.

en: Could you suggest a simple exercise for back pain?
tamil: முதுகு வலிக்கு ஒரு எளிமையான உடற்பயிற்சி சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking a doctor or trainer for advice.
explain: 'Could you suggest ...?' is a polite way to ask for ideas. 'Simple' means easy.
usage: Ask this to a doctor, a gym trainer or a physiotherapist.
leelaQ: Do you sit for a long time? How do you relax your back?
answer: Yes, I sit a lot, so I stand up and walk every hour.

en: Fruits and vegetables are good for your eyes and skin.
tamil: பழங்களும் காய்கறிகளும் கண்ணுக்கும் தோலுக்கும் நல்லது.
context: Giving a general health fact.
explain: 'Good for' tells the benefit of something. Simple present is used for general facts.
usage: Use it when you encourage children or friends to eat healthy.
leelaQ: Which fruit do you like the most?
answer: I like mango the most, especially in summer.

en: I did not have any breakfast today, so I feel weak.
tamil: நான் இன்னைக்கு காலை சாப்பாடே சாப்பிடல, அதனால சோர்வா இருக்கு.
context: Explaining why you feel tired.
explain: 'Did not have' is a past negative. 'So' shows the result.
usage: Say it to a colleague or a friend when you feel low in energy.
leelaQ: What do you eat when you feel weak?
answer: I eat a banana or drink some milk to get energy.

en: Are you trying to lose weight or build muscle?
tamil: நீங்க எடை குறைக்க பாக்குறீங்களா இல்ல மசில் ஏத்தப் பாக்குறீங்களா?
context: A gym trainer asking about your goal.
explain: 'Are you trying to ...?' asks about a goal. 'Or' gives two choices.
usage: A trainer or friend asks this when you start exercising.
leelaQ: What is your main health goal this year?
answer: My goal is to stay fit and walk every day.

en: I have been feeling tired since I changed to the night shift.
tamil: நைட் ஷிஃப்டுக்கு மாறினதிலிருந்து எனக்கு சோர்வா இருக்கு.
context: Telling a doctor about tiredness.
explain: 'Have been feeling' shows a feeling that started in the past and is still going on. 'Since' gives the start.
usage: Use it with a doctor or a manager when work affects your health.
leelaQ: Is it hard to work at night? Why?
answer: Yes, because my body wants to sleep and I feel tired.

en: She should eat more protein, like dal, eggs and paneer.
tamil: அவ பருப்பு, முட்டை, பனீர் மாதிரி இன்னும் அதிகம் புரதம் சாப்பிடணும்.
context: Giving diet advice about someone.
explain: 'Should' gives advice. 'Like' introduces examples.
usage: Use it when you talk about a healthy diet with family.
leelaQ: What protein food do you eat at home?
answer: We eat dal every day and eggs two or three times a week.

en: Let's take the stairs instead of the lift today.
tamil: இன்னைக்கு லிஃப்ட் வேண்டாம், படிக்கட்டுல போகலாம்.
context: Suggesting a small exercise to a colleague.
explain: 'Let's' suggests something to do together. 'Instead of' means in place of.
usage: Say it to a friend or colleague in an office building.
leelaQ: Do you like to use the stairs or the lift?
answer: I use the stairs when it is only two floors.

en: Can I eat sweets if I have diabetes?
tamil: எனக்கு சர்க்கரை நோய் இருந்தா நான் இனிப்பு சாப்பிடலாமா?
context: Asking a doctor about diet rules.
explain: 'Can I ...?' asks for permission. 'If' makes the condition clear.
usage: Ask this to a doctor or a dietitian.
leelaQ: What food should a person with diabetes avoid?
answer: They should avoid sugar, sweets and too much white rice.

en: I sleep better when I switch off my phone early.
tamil: நான் போனை சீக்கிரம் ஆஃப் பண்ணா நல்லா தூங்குவேன்.
context: Sharing a sleep tip with a friend.
explain: 'When' joins a habit and its result. 'Switch off' means to turn off.
usage: Use it when friends say they cannot sleep well.
leelaQ: Do you use your phone before sleeping?
answer: Yes, I watch videos for some time, but I want to stop.

en: Can you tell me a good diet for weight loss?
tamil: எடை குறைக்க ஒரு நல்ல டயட் சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking a dietitian or a friend for a plan.
explain: 'Can you tell me ...?' is a common polite request. 'Diet' means the food plan.
usage: Ask this to a dietitian, a doctor or a fit friend.
leelaQ: What is a healthy dinner for you?
answer: A healthy dinner for me is chapati with vegetable curry.

en: He ran five kilometres without stopping yesterday.
tamil: அவன் நேத்து நிக்காம அஞ்சு கிலோமீட்டர் ஓடினான்.
context: Telling a friend about someone's achievement.
explain: 'Ran' is the past of 'run'. 'Without stopping' means non-stop.
usage: Use it when you praise a friend's fitness.
leelaQ: What is the longest distance you have walked?
answer: I once walked ten kilometres during a temple trip.

en: You must not eat too much junk food, it spoils your stomach.
tamil: நீ ரொம்ப ஜங்க் ஃபுட் சாப்பிடக்கூடாது, அது வயித்தை கெடுக்கும்.
context: Advising a child or a friend.
explain: 'Must not' is a strong rule or advice. 'Spoils' means makes something bad.
usage: Use it with children, younger siblings or friends.
leelaQ: Do you eat junk food? How often?
answer: I eat it once a month, mostly when I go out with friends.

en: I feel very fresh after a good night's sleep.
tamil: நல்லா தூங்கினா நான் ரொம்ப ஃப்ரெஷ்ஷா உணர்வேன்.
context: Telling a colleague about your energy.
explain: 'Feel fresh' means to feel full of energy. 'Good night's sleep' is a fixed phrase.
usage: Say it in a morning chat with friends or colleagues.
leelaQ: How do you feel in the morning after a good sleep?
answer: I feel happy and full of energy, and I start my work early.

en: I am going to cook less oily food from now on.
tamil: நான் இனிமே எண்ணெய் குறைவா சமைக்கப் போறேன்.
context: Telling your family about a diet decision.
explain: 'Am going to' shows a firm plan. 'From now on' means starting today.
usage: Use it when you decide to change your food habits.
leelaQ: What change will you make in your food habits?
answer: I will cook with less oil and add more vegetables.

en: Do you have this medicine in stock?
tamil: இந்த மருந்து உங்க கிட்ட ஸ்டாக்ல இருக்கா?
context: Asking at a medical shop.
explain: 'In stock' means available in the shop. 'Do you have ...?' is a simple shop question.
usage: Use it at a pharmacy when you look for a particular tablet.
leelaQ: What do you ask when a medicine is not available?
answer: I ask if they can order it or tell me a similar medicine.

en: Which doctor should I see for skin problems?
tamil: தோல் பிரச்சனைக்கு நான் எந்த டாக்டரைப் பாக்கணும்?
context: Asking a hospital receptionist.
explain: 'Which ... should I see?' asks for the right choice. 'Skin problems' is a common phrase.
usage: Ask this at the reception of a hospital with many departments.
leelaQ: Which doctor did you see last, and why?
answer: I saw a dentist last month because I had tooth pain.

en: What are the side effects of this tablet?
tamil: இந்த மாத்திரையோட பக்க விளைவுகள் என்ன?
context: Asking a doctor or pharmacist about a medicine.
explain: 'Side effects' are unwanted results of a medicine. 'What are ...?' is used for plural nouns.
usage: Ask this before you start a new medicine.
leelaQ: Do you read the paper that comes with a medicine?
answer: No, I usually do not read it, but I should.

en: Is the doctor available this afternoon?
tamil: இன்னைக்கு மதியம் டாக்டர் இருப்பாரா?
context: Calling a clinic to ask about the doctor.
explain: 'Available' means free and present. 'This afternoon' means today after noon.
usage: Use it on a phone call to a clinic or at the reception.
leelaQ: How do you check if a doctor is free?
answer: I call the clinic and ask the receptionist.

en: How much will the full check-up cost?
tamil: முழு செக்-அப்புக்கு எவ்வளவு செலவாகும்?
context: Asking about hospital charges.
explain: 'How much will ... cost?' asks about price. 'Full' means complete.
usage: Ask this at a hospital counter before you book a test.
leelaQ: Do you think hospital bills are high? Why?
answer: Yes, they are high because tests and medicines are costly.

en: Can I take this tablet on an empty stomach?
tamil: நான் இந்த மாத்திரையை வெறும் வயித்துல சாப்பிடலாமா?
context: Asking a pharmacist.
explain: 'On an empty stomach' means without eating food before. 'Can I ...?' asks for permission.
usage: Ask this at a pharmacy when the tablet has no clear instruction.
leelaQ: What do you eat before taking a tablet?
answer: I eat a biscuit or a banana before I take it.

en: Have you taken your flu vaccine this year?
tamil: இந்த வருஷம் நீங்க ஃப்ளூ தடுப்பூசி போட்டுட்டீங்களா?
context: Asking a colleague or a relative.
explain: 'Have you taken ...?' asks if something is done up to now. 'Vaccine' is the injection that protects.
usage: Use it in an office or family chat during the flu season.
leelaQ: Which vaccines did you take as a child?
answer: I took the polio drops and some injections, my mother says.

en: Shall we go to the hospital together?
tamil: நாம ரெண்டு பேரும் சேர்ந்து ஆஸ்பத்திரிக்கு போகலாமா?
context: Offering company to a sick friend.
explain: 'Shall we ...?' is a polite way to suggest. 'Together' means with each other.
usage: Say it to a friend or relative who is not well.
leelaQ: Who goes with you to the hospital when you are sick?
answer: My brother goes with me, and he waits outside.

en: Please give me a strip of paracetamol.
tamil: எனக்கு ஒரு ஸ்ட்ரிப் பாராசிட்டமால் குடுங்க.
context: Buying a common tablet at a shop.
explain: 'A strip of' is a common way to ask for tablets in India. 'Please' keeps it polite.
usage: Say it at any medical shop.
leelaQ: What medicines do you keep at home?
answer: I keep paracetamol and a cough syrup in my house.

en: Could you reschedule my appointment to Friday?
tamil: என் அப்பாயின்ட்மென்ட்டை வெள்ளிக்கிழமைக்கு மாத்த முடியுமா?
context: Calling a clinic to change a booking.
explain: 'Reschedule' means to change the time. 'Could you ...?' is polite and formal.
usage: Use it on a call or at the desk when your plan changes.
leelaQ: What will you say if you cannot go to an appointment?
answer: I will call and ask them to change it to another day.

en: Please show your report to the doctor tomorrow.
tamil: நாளைக்கு உங்க ரிப்போர்ட்டை டாக்டர் கிட்ட காட்டுங்க.
context: A lab staff giving an instruction.
explain: 'Show ... to ...' is the correct pattern. 'Please' makes the order soft.
usage: Lab staff or family may say this after a test.
leelaQ: Where do you keep your medical reports?
answer: I keep them in a file at home in a cupboard.

en: Can you give me a cough syrup for children?
tamil: குழந்தைகளுக்கான இருமல் சிரப் குடுக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking at a pharmacy.
explain: 'For children' tells who will use it. 'Can you give me ...?' is a simple polite request.
usage: Use it at a pharmacy when you buy medicine for kids.
leelaQ: What do you do when a child has a cough?
answer: I give warm water and take the child to a doctor.

en: This tablet is not available in our shop right now.
tamil: இந்த மாத்திரை இப்போ எங்க கடையில இல்ல.
context: A pharmacist giving news to a customer.
explain: 'Not available' means we do not have it. 'Right now' means at this moment.
usage: A shopkeeper or a pharmacist says this to a customer.
leelaQ: What will you do if a shop does not have what you need?
answer: I will try another shop or order it online.

en: You should not stop the antibiotics in the middle.
tamil: நீங்க ஆன்டிபயாடிக்கை நடுவுல நிறுத்தக்கூடாது.
context: A doctor or pharmacist warning a patient.
explain: 'Should not' gives a strong warning. 'In the middle' means before the course is finished.
usage: Doctors and pharmacists say this to avoid problems later.
leelaQ: Why is it important to finish a medicine course?
answer: It is important because the sickness may come back.

en: I want to book an appointment with a dentist.
tamil: நான் ஒரு பல் டாக்டர் கிட்ட அப்பாயின்ட்மென்ட் புக் பண்ணணும்.
context: Calling a dental clinic.
explain: 'Want to book' is a clear way to say your need. 'Dentist' is a tooth doctor.
usage: Use it on a call or at the reception of a clinic.
leelaQ: Do you go to the dentist often?
answer: No, I go only when I have tooth pain.

en: The doctor has asked me to come for a follow-up next week.
tamil: டாக்டர் அடுத்த வாரம் ஃபாலோ-அப்புக்கு வரச் சொல்லியிருக்காரு.
context: Telling your boss why you need leave.
explain: 'Has asked me to come' reports the doctor's instruction. 'Follow-up' is a repeat visit.
usage: Say it to a manager or family when you plan the next week.
leelaQ: When will you visit the doctor next?
answer: I will visit the doctor next Saturday morning.

en: My appointment is at half past four this evening.
tamil: என் அப்பாயின்ட்மென்ட் இன்னைக்கு சாயங்காலம் நாலரை மணிக்கு.
context: Telling a colleague when you will leave.
explain: 'Half past four' means 4:30. 'Is at' gives the fixed time.
usage: Use it when you need to leave work early.
leelaQ: What time is your next important meeting or appointment?
answer: It is at ten tomorrow morning at my office.

en: I have lost my prescription, so I need a copy.
tamil: என் பிரிஸ்கிரிப்ஷன் தொலைஞ்சிடுச்சு, அதனால ஒரு காப்பி வேணும்.
context: Asking a clinic or a hospital for a new copy.
explain: 'Have lost' shows the result now: you do not have it. 'So' gives the reason.
usage: Use it at a clinic or a medical shop when you lose papers.
leelaQ: What will you do if you lose an important paper?
answer: I will look at home first and then ask for a new copy.

en: You will feel better in two or three days.
tamil: ரெண்டு மூணு நாள்ல உங்களுக்கு நல்லா இருக்கும்.
context: A doctor giving hope to a patient.
explain: 'Will feel' predicts the future. 'Two or three days' is a common loose number.
usage: Doctors or elders say this to comfort a sick person.
leelaQ: How can you cheer up a friend who is sick?
answer: I can visit him, bring fruits and talk to him for some time.

en: I got my eyes tested and I need new glasses now.
tamil: நான் கண் பரிசோதனை பண்ணினேன், இப்போ புது கண்ணாடி வேணும்.
context: Telling a friend about an eye check.
explain: 'Got my eyes tested' means someone else did the test for you. 'Need' shows a present need.
usage: Use it when you talk about your eyesight or a new spectacle.
leelaQ: Do you wear glasses? Since when?
answer: Yes, I have worn glasses since I was in school.

en: The doctor is seeing another patient right now.
tamil: டாக்டர் இப்போ இன்னொரு பேஷண்டைப் பாத்துட்டு இருக்காரு.
context: A nurse telling you to wait.
explain: 'Is seeing' shows what is happening now. 'See a patient' means to treat a patient.
usage: Nurses and receptionists say this in a waiting hall.
leelaQ: What do you do while you wait in a clinic?
answer: I sit quietly and read a magazine or use my phone.

en: My grandfather is in the hospital, but he is recovering well.
tamil: எங்க தாத்தா ஆஸ்பத்திரில இருக்காரு, ஆனா நல்லா குணமாகிட்டு வராரு.
context: Giving news about a family member.
explain: 'But' joins two opposite ideas. 'Is recovering' shows slow improvement.
usage: Use it when friends or colleagues ask about your family.
leelaQ: How do you take care of an elder person at home?
answer: I give him food on time and sit with him in the evening.

en: I always keep a first-aid box at home.
tamil: நான் எப்பவும் வீட்டுல ஒரு முதலுதவி பெட்டி வச்சிருப்பேன்.
context: Talking about being ready for small injuries.
explain: 'Always' comes before the main verb. A first-aid box has bandages and basic medicine.
usage: Use it in a talk about safety at home.
leelaQ: What things are in your first-aid box?
answer: There are a bandage, cotton, an ointment and a few tablets.

en: The report will be ready by tomorrow afternoon.
tamil: ரிப்போர்ட் நாளைக்கு மதியத்துக்குள்ள ரெடியாகிடும்.
context: A lab staff giving the delivery time.
explain: 'By' means not later than. 'Will be ready' gives the future state.
usage: Lab and hospital staff use this sentence with patients.
leelaQ: How do you collect your test reports?
answer: I collect them at the counter or get them by email.

en: I twisted my ankle while playing cricket yesterday.
tamil: நான் நேத்து கிரிக்கெட் விளையாடும்போது கணுக்கால் சுளுக்கிடுச்சு.
context: Explaining an injury to a doctor.
explain: 'While playing' tells what you were doing. 'Twisted' is the past of 'twist'.
usage: Use it with a doctor or friends when you have a sports injury.
leelaQ: Have you ever hurt yourself while playing?
answer: Yes, I fell down and hurt my knee while playing football.

en: Are you feeling dizzy or weak?
tamil: உங்களுக்கு தலை சுத்துதா இல்ல சோர்வா இருக்கா?
context: A doctor asking about symptoms.
explain: 'Dizzy' means the head feels like spinning. 'Or' offers two symptoms to choose from.
usage: A doctor or a nurse asks this at a check-up.
leelaQ: How do you feel when you are very tired?
answer: I feel weak, and I cannot focus on my work.

en: Where does it hurt exactly?
tamil: சரியா எங்க வலிக்குது?
context: A doctor asking about pain.
explain: 'Exactly' asks for the exact spot. 'Hurt' is a verb for pain.
usage: A doctor or physiotherapist asks this to find the pain.
leelaQ: Can you show where you had pain last time?
answer: I had pain in my lower back, near the waist.

en: Did you eat anything unusual last night?
tamil: நேத்து ராத்திரி ஏதாவது வித்தியாசமா சாப்பிட்டீங்களா?
context: A doctor asking about stomach trouble.
explain: 'Anything unusual' means something not normal. 'Did you eat ...?' asks about the past.
usage: Doctors ask this when a patient has stomach pain or loose motion.
leelaQ: What did you eat for dinner yesterday?
answer: I ate chapati and dal with a little rice.

en: When should I come back for the next check-up?
tamil: அடுத்த செக்-அப்புக்கு நான் எப்போ திரும்ப வரணும்?
context: Asking a doctor before leaving.
explain: 'Come back' means return. 'Should I' asks for the doctor's advice.
usage: Ask this at the end of a visit to the doctor.
leelaQ: What do you ask the doctor before leaving the room?
answer: I ask about the food rules and the next visit date.

en: Do you do any exercise at home?
tamil: நீங்க வீட்டுல ஏதாவது உடற்பயிற்சி பண்றீங்களா?
context: A doctor or friend asking about your lifestyle.
explain: 'Do you do ...?' asks about a habit. 'Any' makes the question open.
usage: A doctor or a trainer asks this to learn about your lifestyle.
leelaQ: Do you do any exercise at home? Which one?
answer: Yes, I do simple stretching for ten minutes every morning.

en: Will I need an injection?
tamil: எனக்கு ஊசி போடணுமா?
context: Asking a doctor, a bit nervously.
explain: 'Will I need ...?' asks if something will be required. It is short and polite.
usage: Say it to a doctor or a nurse when you feel afraid.
leelaQ: Are you afraid of injections? Why?
answer: Yes, a little, because I do not like the pain.

en: What did the doctor say about your report?
tamil: உங்க ரிப்போர்ட் பத்தி டாக்டர் என்ன சொன்னாரு?
context: Asking a friend or relative after their visit.
explain: 'What did ... say' asks about past words. The verb 'say' stays in base form.
usage: Use it with a friend or family member who went for a test.
leelaQ: How do you feel when you wait for a test result?
answer: I feel nervous until the doctor says everything is normal.

en: How is your father's health now?
tamil: உங்க அப்பாவோட உடம்பு இப்போ எப்படி இருக்கு?
context: Asking about a colleague's family member.
explain: 'How is ... now?' is a polite way to ask about recovery. 'Health' is a noun.
usage: Use it in an office or neighbourhood when you care about someone.
leelaQ: How is your family's health these days?
answer: Everyone is fine, thank God, and we are all busy.

en: Please open your mouth and say aaah.
tamil: வாயைத் திறந்து ஆஹ்னு சொல்லுங்க.
context: A doctor checking your throat.
explain: Two imperatives are joined with 'and'. Doctors use simple commands like this.
usage: Doctors say this during a throat check-up.
leelaQ: What does a doctor check first when you have a cold?
answer: He checks my throat, my nose and my temperature.

en: Could you speak a little slower, doctor?
tamil: கொஞ்சம் மெதுவா பேச முடியுமா டாக்டர்?
context: Asking a doctor to repeat clearly.
explain: 'A little slower' is a soft way to ask. 'Could you' makes it polite.
usage: Use it when someone speaks fast and you cannot follow.
leelaQ: What do you do when you do not understand something?
answer: I ask the person to repeat it slowly.

en: Breathe in slowly and then breathe out.
tamil: மெதுவா மூச்சை உள்ள இழுத்து அப்புறம் வெளியே விடுங்க.
context: A doctor listening to your chest.
explain: 'Breathe in' and 'breathe out' are phrasal verbs. 'Slowly' tells how to do it.
usage: Doctors, nurses and yoga teachers give this instruction.
leelaQ: When do you take deep breaths?
answer: I take deep breaths when I feel stressed or angry.

en: Can you take me to the hospital right now?
tamil: நீ இப்போவே என்னை ஆஸ்பத்திரிக்கு கூட்டிட்டுப் போக முடியுமா?
context: Asking a family member in an urgent case.
explain: 'Right now' shows urgency. 'Take me to' means to go with me and drop me.
usage: Say it to family or a neighbour in an emergency.
leelaQ: Who will you call if you need help at night?
answer: I will call my brother or a neighbour who has a car.

en: I do not eat non-veg food during fasting days.
tamil: நான் விரத நாட்கள்ல அசைவம் சாப்பிட மாட்டேன்.
context: Explaining a food rule to a colleague.
explain: 'Do not eat' is a present negative. 'Non-veg' is a short form of non-vegetarian.
usage: Use it politely when someone offers you food on a fasting day.
leelaQ: What food do you avoid and why?
answer: I avoid very spicy food because it upsets my stomach.

en: I have never taken any sleeping pills.
tamil: நான் இதுவரைக்கும் தூக்க மாத்திரை எடுத்ததே இல்ல.
context: Telling a doctor about your history.
explain: 'Have never taken' talks about your whole life up to now. 'Any' stresses none.
usage: Say it when a doctor asks about medicines you took before.
leelaQ: What natural way do you use to fall asleep?
answer: I drink warm milk and listen to soft music.

en: I get a headache whenever I sit before the computer too long.
tamil: கம்ப்யூட்டர் முன்னாடி ரொம்ப நேரம் உக்கார்ந்தா எனக்கு தலைவலி வரும்.
context: Explaining your problem to a doctor.
explain: 'Whenever' means every time. It joins a habit and its result.
usage: Use it with a doctor or an optician when you describe your problem.
leelaQ: Do you work on a computer? How do you rest your eyes?
answer: Yes, I look away for a minute after every hour.

en: It is only a mild infection, so there is nothing to worry about.
tamil: இது சின்ன இன்ஃபெக்ஷன் தான், அதனால கவலைப்பட ஒண்ணும் இல்ல.
context: A doctor calming a patient.
explain: 'Mild' means not serious. 'Nothing to worry about' is a comforting phrase.
usage: Doctors or elders use it to comfort someone who is anxious.
leelaQ: What do you say to a person who is worried about health?
answer: I tell them to relax and follow the doctor's advice.

en: I stayed in bed the whole day because of the fever.
tamil: காய்ச்சல் காரணமா நான் நாள் முழுக்க படுக்கையிலேயே இருந்தேன்.
context: Telling a friend why you did not call.
explain: 'Because of' is followed by a noun. 'The whole day' means all day.
usage: Use it to explain why you missed work or a call.
leelaQ: What do you do on a day when you are sick?
answer: I rest at home, drink hot soup and watch some TV.

en: The pain has reduced a lot after the injection.
tamil: ஊசி போட்டதுக்கு அப்புறம் வலி ரொம்ப குறைஞ்சிடுச்சு.
context: Telling the doctor how you feel.
explain: 'Has reduced' shows a change with a result now. 'A lot' means very much.
usage: Say it in a follow-up visit or when family asks about your health.
leelaQ: How do you feel when your pain goes away?
answer: I feel relaxed and happy, and I start doing my work again.

en: My neighbour is a doctor, so we ask him for small problems.
tamil: எங்க பக்கத்து வீட்டுக்காரர் டாக்டர், அதனால சின்ன பிரச்சனைனா அவர் கிட்ட கேப்போம்.
context: Talking about a helpful neighbour.
explain: 'So' joins a reason and a result. 'Small problems' means minor health issues.
usage: Use it in a talk about community and support.
leelaQ: Do you have a helpful neighbour? How do they help?
answer: Yes, my neighbour helps us when we need a lift or a tool.

en: I will ask my wife to prepare light food for dinner.
tamil: நான் ராத்திரிக்கு லேசான சாப்பாடு செய்யச் சொல்லி என் மனைவிகிட்ட கேக்கறேன்.
context: Telling a doctor or friend about diet changes.
explain: 'Will ask ... to ...' shows a plan. 'Light food' means easy-to-digest food.
usage: Use it when you plan to eat simple food after an illness.
leelaQ: What light food do you eat when you are sick?
answer: I eat rice porridge or idli with a little chutney.

en: Many people in my office have caught the viral fever.
tamil: எங்க ஆபீஸ்ல நிறைய பேருக்கு வைரல் காய்ச்சல் பிடிச்சிருக்கு.
context: Telling a friend about an illness at work.
explain: 'Have caught' is used with a fever or cold. 'Many people' is a plural subject.
usage: Use it when you talk about a seasonal illness.
leelaQ: What do you do to stay safe in the rainy season?
answer: I drink boiled water and avoid street food.

en: I am going to take two days' leave for my health.
tamil: நான் என் உடம்புக்காக ரெண்டு நாள் லீவு எடுக்கப் போறேன்.
context: Telling a manager you need rest.
explain: 'Am going to take' shows a plan. 'Leave' means a break from work.
usage: Say it to a manager, a teacher or a friend when you need rest.
leelaQ: Do you take leave when you are not well?
answer: Yes, I take one or two days so that I can recover fully.

en: Walking after dinner helps with digestion.
tamil: சாப்பிட்ட பிறகு நடந்தா செரிமானம் நல்லா இருக்கும்.
context: Giving a health tip to a friend.
explain: 'Walking' acts as a noun here. 'Helps with' shows the benefit.
usage: Use it as friendly advice in a talk about health.
leelaQ: Do you walk after dinner? For how long?
answer: Yes, I walk for fifteen minutes near my house.

en: My sister is waiting outside the doctor's room.
tamil: என் தங்கை டாக்டர் ரூமுக்கு வெளியே காத்துட்டு இருக்கா.
context: Telling a nurse who is with you.
explain: 'Is waiting' shows an action in progress. 'Outside' tells the place.
usage: Say it at a hospital to explain who has come with you.
leelaQ: Who comes with you when you visit a hospital?
answer: My sister usually comes with me and carries my file.

en: Health is more important than money, so take care.
tamil: உடம்பு தான் பணத்தை விட முக்கியம், அதனால பாத்துக்கோங்க.
context: Advising a friend who works too much.
explain: 'More ... than' compares two things. 'Take care' is a warm closing phrase.
usage: Use it kindly with a friend who ignores their health.
leelaQ: What is more important to you, health or money? Why?
answer: Health is more important, because I need it for everything.
